platforms.title: Blood Clots From Sitting: Why Long Trips Raise the Risk
platforms.meta_description: A DVT clot doesn't need a plane — just hours of not moving your calves. What the CDC and travel-medicine research say about risk and real prevention.
platforms.body_html:
People tend to blame blood clots on flying itself. But according to the CDC, anyone traveling more than four hours by air, car, bus, or train can be at risk — the plane isn't the cause, hours of not moving your legs is.

Why Sitting Still Is What Actually Causes It

Your calf muscles work as a pump: every time you walk or flex them, they squeeze blood in the leg veins back up toward the heart. When that pump goes idle for hours, blood pools and can start to clot. The CDC notes that the risk is real but low for healthy travelers — about 2 out of 10,000 people develop a clot with noticeable symptoms after a flight longer than four hours. Risk climbs for people with additional factors: recent surgery, active cancer, pregnancy or the recent postpartum period, hormone therapy, obesity, or a previous history of a blood clot.

Research reviewed in the Cochrane Library on airline passengers found a striking gap: in one set of studies, symptomless DVT showed up in a share of passengers who wore no compression stockings, while almost none of the passengers wearing them developed one — a difference large enough that compression stockings are now a standard recommendation for medium- and high-risk travelers specifically, not for every passenger.

Symptoms That Mean Go to the ER, Not Wait

Swelling in one leg only, pain when you press on it, or skin that feels warm or looks red is worth taking seriously. Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain can mean the clot has moved to the lungs — that combination is a medical emergency, not something to self-manage or wait out.

3 Habits That Actually Cut the Risk

  • Get up and move every hour. Walk the aisle when you can, and when you can't, flex your ankles up and down repeatedly in your seat — this restarts the calf pump even while seated.
  • Stay hydrated and skip alcohol and heavy caffeine. Both are diuretics that thicken your blood further on top of travel dehydration.
  • Wear graduated compression stockings if you have any risk factor. Knee-high stockings in the 15–30 mmHg range are the level studied for travel-related clot prevention — not the mild support socks sold as general comfort wear.

It Was Never Really About the Plane

A blood clot from travel isn't caused by altitude or cabin pressure — it's caused by your calf pump sitting idle for hours, on a plane, bus, or even at a desk. If one leg suddenly swells and hurts, or you feel short of breath afterward, don't wait it out — get seen the same day. This article is general health information, not a diagnosis; talk to a clinician about your personal risk factors before a long trip — smoking, pregnancy, hormone therapy, recent surgery, and a past clot, and simply being over 60 all raise the odds enough to plan ahead with your doctor rather than find out somewhere over the middle of the ocean.
